title: Heaps of Offerings: Providing for the Temple's Servants
summary: After the Passover, the worshipers go out and destroy the pillars, Asherah poles, and high places throughout Judah and even in the north. Hezekiah reorganizes the priests and Levites, gives from his own flocks for the regular sacrifices, and calls the people to support the temple's ministers. The people bring firstfruits and tithes in such abundance that heaps pile up for four months, and Hezekiah appoints faithful Levites to store and distribute them fairly to every priestly and Levitical family.
story: Chapter 29 cleansed the temple and chapter 30 gathered the people to worship there. This chapter makes the reform last. Joy at a festival is one thing; sustaining a ministry through ordinary months is another. Hezekiah puts the temple on a stable footing, as David and Solomon had done in organizing its service. The chapter ends with a summary verdict that Hezekiah did what was "good and upright and true" and that he prospered (verses 20-21). That verdict is placed deliberately before the next chapter, where the Assyrian king Sennacherib invades. Faithfulness does not exempt Hezekiah from crisis, but it prepares him for it.
historical:
The parallel in Kings is brief: 2 Kings 18:4 says Hezekiah removed the high places, broke the pillars, cut down the Asherah, and destroyed the bronze serpent Moses had made, because people had been burning incense to it. The Assyrian officer who later taunted Jerusalem mentions the removal of the high places as though it had angered the LORD (2 Kings 18:22), which suggests the reform was well known and controversial. Some archaeologists have linked the dismantling of a horned altar at Beersheba and changes at the shrine at Arad to Hezekiah's centralization of worship, though the dating and interpretation of those finds are disputed.

Verse 1 says the destruction reached Ephraim and Manasseh, territory of the former northern kingdom. After Samaria's fall that land was under Assyrian administration, and how far Judean influence could reach there is uncertain. The Chronicler presents the purge as the act of the returning worshipers, the Israelites who had been at the feast, rather than an official royal campaign.
cultural:
Under the Law, the priests and Levites received no tribal land. Instead the LORD was their inheritance, and they lived on the tithes and offerings of the other tribes (Numbers 18:20-24). When the people neglected these gifts, the Levites had to leave the temple and work their fields, and the service collapsed (compare Nehemiah 13:10). Hezekiah's command in verse 4 restores the system so that the ministers could "devote themselves to the Law of the LORD."

Firstfruits were the first and best of the harvest, given to God in acknowledgment that the whole crop was his gift. The timing in verse 7 follows the agricultural year: the third month was the time of the wheat harvest and the Feast of Weeks, and the seventh month brought the grape and olive harvests and the Feast of Tabernacles. The heaps grew through an entire harvest season. Storerooms in the temple complex held such goods, and careful records, including genealogies, determined who was entitled to a share. Children as young as three were counted, and families were included, so the distribution reached whole households.
literary: The chapter moves from destruction (verse 1) to organization (verses 2-4), to generosity (verses 5-10), to administration (verses 11-19), and closes with a theological summary (verses 20-21). The word translated faithfully or faithfulness recurs in verses 12, 15, and 18, describing both those who brought the gifts and those who handled them. The long lists of names in verses 12-15 are not filler; they show that the gifts were managed by accountable, named people. The final verses give Hezekiah one of the fullest commendations in Chronicles, using the vocabulary of seeking God and prospering that runs through the whole book.

outline.t: Idolatrous shrines destroyed across the land
Priestly divisions restored and support commanded
Firstfruits and tithes pile up in heaps

doctrines.note: Hezekiah provides for the daily, weekly, monthly, and festival sacrifices. Worship in the Old Testament had a regular rhythm, and the chapter shows that sustaining it was a shared responsibility of king and people.

The people support those who serve God full time, and the gifts are distributed fairly and transparently. The chapter models a community that provides for its ministers and manages its resources with integrity.
The chief priest explains the surplus simply: the LORD has blessed his people. The abundance is both the people's gift and God's provision.

words.note: Maaser, tithe, a tenth. The Law required a tenth of produce and livestock to support the Levites and the temple (Leviticus 27:30-32; Numbers 18:21). Here the tithe returns after years of neglect, brought from both Judah and the northern refugees living in Judah.
Reshit, first or beginning, here the firstfruits. Giving the first portion rather than the leftovers expressed trust that God would provide the rest of the harvest.

Emunah, faithfulness or trustworthiness. The same root gives the word amen. The Levites handle the gifts faithfully, which in context means honestly and reliably. The chapter treats good administration as a spiritual virtue.

Terumah, contribution. The word refers to a portion set apart and lifted up for God, often used for gifts that went to the priests. It stresses that the offering is removed from ordinary use and dedicated.

christ: The New Testament draws on this pattern of support for God's servants. Paul reminds the Corinthians that those who serve at the altar share in what is offered on the altar, and that the Lord commanded those who proclaim the gospel to live by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:13-14). The generous, willing giving of the people also anticipates the early church in Jerusalem, where believers brought their gifts and distribution was made to each as any had need (Acts 4:34-35). Hezekiah's summary, that he did what was good, upright, and true before God, describes a king who sought God in everything; the Gospels present Jesus as the Son who always does what pleases his Father (John 8:29). These links are thematic, not predictive.

hard.q: Does this chapter mean Christians today are required to tithe?
hard.a: Christians answer this in different ways. Some hold that the tithe predates the Law (Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek in Genesis 14:20) and remains a standard for God's people. Others argue that the tithe belonged to the temple system of Israel, which Christ fulfilled, and that the New Testament replaces a fixed percentage with generous, cheerful, proportionate giving (2 Corinthians 9:6-7), which may be more or less than a tenth. Both sides agree on what this chapter plainly shows: God's people are to give their first and best, to support those who serve in ministry, and to handle gifts faithfully. How the specific tenth applies is a second-order question on which faithful believers differ.

questions: The people's generosity was so great that the leftovers piled up in heaps. What would it take for your giving to be marked by that kind of overflow?
The gifts were handled by named, faithful people with clear responsibilities. How can churches and ministries today show that same integrity with money?
Hezekiah was diligent in every work he began in order to seek his God. What unfinished work of devotion might God be calling you to complete?
